title: Remarks: A Reset on Liquidity Regulation
summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent and Under Secretary McKernan outlined a fundamental reset of bank liquidity regulation, arguing that post-2008 liquidity rules have unnecessarily constrained banks' lending capacity. The speech identified that approximately 25% of large banks' balance sheets are now allocated to safe assets (up from roughly 10% pre-crisis), and called for reforms that would unlock hundreds of billions to potentially trillions of dollars in new lending capacity for AI infrastructure, domestic supply chains, and the defense industrial base.
key_points: Post-2008 liquidity regulation was described as 'muddled guesswork' and 'overcorrection written in the dark shadow of the crisis' that requires reassessment.
Current framework allocates roughly 25% of large banks' balance sheets to safe assets, up from approximately 10% before 2008—a shift that reduces lending capacity.
The March 2023 banking stress (SVB, Signature, First Republic) revealed that Treasury and agency MBS holdings were only liquid 'on paper' because collateral was not fully prepositioned.
Discount window stigma is entrenched by the framework itself: banks avoid using it until conditions are severe, so usage signals distress.
The Treasury is coordinating a regulatory reset including modernization of bank capital rules to end 'capital arbitrage that drives financial activity to nonbanks.'
Near-term reforms will focus on reducing discount window stigma, incentivizing collateral prepositioning, and normalizing routine testing of central bank facilities.
why_it_matters: This speech signals a significant shift in regulatory philosophy toward bank liquidity requirements. If implemented, proposed reforms could materially alter how banks allocate their balance sheets, potentially freeing up substantial lending capacity. The discussion of lender of last resort normalization is particularly relevant given the March 2023 stress episode. Market participants should monitor for concrete regulatory proposals, as changes could affect bank profitability, Treasury demand, and the relative attractiveness of bank vs. nonbank lending.
macro_context: The speech explicitly connects regulatory reset to financing needs for AI infrastructure, onshoring of manufacturing, and defense industrial base. It frames liquidity reform as essential to unlocking 'hundreds of billions—potentially trillions—in new lending capacity' for these macroeconomic priorities. The speech also references 'Golden Age' rhetoric tied to the current administration's economic agenda.
market_structure_context: The speech addresses the mechanics of liquidity regulation: buffer useability, discount window operations, collateral prepositioning, and the role of the lender of last resort. It critiques the post-2008 framework for creating 'buffer hoarding' dynamics that can accelerate (rather than absorb) liquidity stress transmission. The upshot is a potential restructuring of how banks manage reserve requirements and access Federal Reserve facilities.
